detail.abstract: This paper introduces Reinforcement Learning from Reputation Feedback (RLRF), an alignment mechanism that replaces the human annotator panel of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) with an economically incentivized validation pool of computative agents whose members stake non-transferable reputation. The paper grounds the mechanism in the Computative Economics framework (Kaal 2026), in which the analytical primitive is a computative agent characterized by the tuple and the object of analysis is a generated possibility space from which realizations are drawn. Under this framing, the paper takes the conceptual position that RLHF applies a scarcity-economic primitive to a signal-generation task that is computative in nature.

detail.title: Digital Platform Usage and its Influence on Workplace Communication Effectiveness in a Philippine Government Office

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest in the conduct and writing of this research. Likewise, the authors have no competing interests to declare relevant to this article’s content.

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of digital platforms has reshaped workplace communication in public sector organizations. Anchored on Media Richness Theory, this study examined how digital platform usage influences workplace communication effectiveness in a Philippine government office. Using a descriptive quantitative research design, data were collected from 155 permanent government employees using a validated survey questionnaire and analyzed through descriptive statistics and Spearman's rank-order correlation. Findings revealed that digital platforms are generally highly utilized for information dissemination, collaboration, relationship building, and task coordination. On the other hand, workplace communication effectiveness is also rated high. The study also found out that digital platform usage is significantly related to workplace communication effectiveness, with frequency of platform use showing a comparatively weaker effect compared with purpose of usage. Despite the importance of digital platform usage, challenges persist such as information overload, privacy concerns, and work-life boundary issues. Grounded on these findings, the researchers proposed strategies to enhance digital platform usage and workplace communication effectiveness in the subject government office. Consistent with Media Richness Theory, the findings indicate that workplace communication effectiveness is driven more by the richness and quality of communication particularly by its clarity, responsiveness, and feedback, than by the mere intensity of platform usage. The findings provide empirical insights that may guide communication policy development, leadership practices, and digital governance initiatives in Philippine government institutions.

detail.abstract: Firms increasingly deploy large language models (LLMs) to screen job applications, while applicants increasingly use LLMs to write their resumes. This paper provides the first systematic empirical test of whether the choice of resume-writing model affects hiring outcomes, holding qualifications constant. We construct 100 synthetic but realistic candidate profiles spanning 12 industries and four career levels, each matched to a tailored job posting. For every profile, four functionally identical resumes are generated by GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3 Pro, and xAI Grok 4.3, varying only in language, structure, and phrasing. Each of the resulting 400 resumes is then evaluated blind by all four models, yielding 1,576 valid evaluations (98.5% of 1,600 possible data points) on a 0–100 fit score and a categorical hire / maybe / reject recommendation. Applying a strict binary standard in which only an explicit “hire” counts as a positive outcome, we document hire-rate gaps of up to 42 percentage points for the identical candidate depending solely on which model wrote the resume, and a 29-point score gap between two evaluators reading the identical document. Claude Sonnet 4.6 exhibits the strongest positive self-preference (84% for its own style versus 42% for GPT-authored resumes), while GPT5.4 shows a negative self-bias, rating its own writing style lowest among the four (82% versus 97% for Gemini-authored resumes). Gemini 3 Pro produces the most universally rewarded format across all four evaluators. These findings imply that single-model automated screening systematically disadvantages qualified candidates on the basis of writing style rather than substance, with direct implications for employment discrimination risk, EU AI Act Article 13 transparency obligations, and career-counseling practice.

detail.title: Development and Validation of a Digital Clinical Management Platform for a Maxillofacial Surgery Department
detail.abstract: Background and objective: Surgical departments with clinical documen-tation needs not fully addressed by transversal hospital information systemsoften continue to rely on manual, paper-based registration of surgical pro-cedures, with clinical photographs stored without structured organization ordirect association with the corresponding records. This fragmented approachhinders information retrieval and compromises data traceability. This studyaimed to design, develop and validate MaxiLog, a full-code digital clinicalmanagement platform tailored to the workflow of a maxillofacial surgery de-partment.Methods: Requirements were generated through an iterative, user-centeredprocess, combining clinical workflow analysis with regular meetings withhealthcare professionals. A full-code web application was developed and inte-grated with the institution’s existing patient information and authenticationsystems. The platform was incrementally validated throughout developmentand subsequently evaluated by healthcare professionals through functionaltests, a standardized usability assessment, and a satisfaction questionnaire.Results: The resulting platform supports registration and consultationof surgical procedures, structured management of clinical photographs, achronological patient timeline, advanced search, reversible deletion and re-covery of records and photographs, automatic identification of incompleterecords, and department-level activity statistics. All prioritized functionalrequirements were implemented and validated. Evaluation with healthcareprofessionals showed high satisfaction, and participants unanimously agreedthat the platform represents a significant improvement over the previouspaper-based process.Conclusions: The proposed platform replaces a previous low-code pro-totype that was not adopted in clinical practice, demonstrating that a full-code approach better addressed the department’s requirements. The systemimproves information traceability and accessibility, providing a flexible tech-nological foundation for future integration with the broader hospital infor-mation ecosystem.

title: Securing AI Is Not Governing It: The Detectability Asymmetry in Enterprise AI Governance

detail.title: Securing AI Is Not Governing It: The Detectability Asymmetry in Enterprise AI Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I (The author) have filed provisional patent applications with IP Australia (2026904061, 2026904062) relating to the privacy-preserving routing work cited in Section 5 of the paper. This interest is also disclosed in the paper itself. No other personal or financial relationships influenced this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by me (the author).

detail.abstract: The governance of enterprise AI has matured in one dimension only. A dense body of security and risk guidance — NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, MITRE ATLAS — catalogues how deployed systems expand the attack surface: the exposures they introduce and the unsanctioned actions they can be induced to take. Whether the same adoption delivers value goes largely unmeasured and ungoverned. We argue this imbalance is consequential and self-reinforcing: because governance instruments the harm a system can enable but not the value it can quietly cease to deliver, ungoverned adoption proliferates in ways that, in turn, enlarge the attack surface. The gap is sustained by vocabulary: guardrail denotes, almost without exception, a control that prevents harm. We introduce a second class — value guardrails, which govern whether a deployed system remains worth operating — and distinguish them from runtime model monitoring, which scores technical quality against fixed references rather than value against an evolving strategy. We characterize, through signal detection theory, a detectability asymmetry: security failures tend to surface as discrete, high-signal events, whereas value failures accumulate as low-signal drift that no incident announces. This asymmetry has two components: an intrinsic one, in how separable each failure type is from operational noise, and an institutional one, in the detection apparatus, ownership, and disclosure obligations built for security and not value. Only the institutional component is readily remediable. We present a conceptual framework whose contribution is threefold: the guardrail distinction, the detectability asymmetry, and the diagnosis that the security and value literatures remain largely disjoint. We then draw the implications for organizations that set both guardrails as coupled levers of AI strategy.

detail.abstract: When a person and a large language model appear to understand one another-to share, in some measure, the same concept-what has actually crossed between them, and what has not? This paper argues for a descriptive asymmetry: the relational structure of a representation, its how, transfers across a shared form, while its grounded, life-indexed content, its what, does not. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis is read not as an objection but as evidence for one half of this claim, and constitutively silent on the other-the metrics that establish representational convergence are relational, and register only how. The asymmetry is located in a single criterion: whether a system's states have a reproducible core beneath their variation. Four consequences follow. The what is distinguished from a merely higher-resolution how, against the embodied-AI reply and the functionalism behind it (§1). The residue left in any transmission, familiar since Quine, is shown to be old in itself but newly concealed when machine fluency removes the friction by which residue was detected (§2). The resulting drift of human cognition toward the machine's geometry is traced, together with the condition under which it can be resisted-possession of an axis, a life-anchored point of collation, itself the non-reproducible what (§3). Finally, a levelling dynamics is argued to concentrate rather than extinguish the what, since only the reproducible can be levelled, so that the very novelty a self-training system requires is, in its non-reproducible part, what it cannot itself produce (§4). The claims are structural, defeasible, and scoped to computational systems with a copyable, resettable core. The paper discloses its own reliance on AI translation as an instance of the asymmetry it describes.

title: Autonomous Micro-Enterprise Governance (AMEG): Architectural Accountability, Deontic-Epistemic Verification, and Statutory Auditability in Multi-Agent Systems

detail.title: Autonomous Micro-Enterprise Governance (AMEG): Architectural Accountability, Deontic-Epistemic Verification, and Statutory Auditability in Multi-Agent Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
As autonomous multi-agent generative systems transition from conversational prototypes to high-stakes revenue-bearing infrastructure, organizational accountability can no longer rely on extrinsic policy documents audited ex-post. This paper formalizes Autonomous Micro-Enterprise Governance, an architectural runtime framework that embeds institutional governance and statutory mandates directly into the state-transition dynamics of autonomous firms.

Extending the Autonomous Micro-Enterprise Architecture state-machine model, it establishes an institutionally regulated eight-tuple combining state spaces, agent actions, transition functions, environmental streams, deontic constraint lattices, settlement primitives, epistemic registries, and execution ledgers. Institutional policies are formalized as a dynamic deontic constraint lattice of obligations, permissions, and prohibitions combined with multi-agent epistemic state tracking, evaluated via a deterministic validation predicate prior to external settlement dispatch.

To operationalize the EU AI Act, specifically Title III requirements for high-risk systems under Articles 9, 11, 12, 14, and 15, discrete state mutations are recorded in a cryptographic, tamper-evident Merkle execution tree, guaranteeing mathematical auditability and causal traceability without persisting unbounded natural-language logs. We prove that under a sound normative lattice and bounded self-correction refinement, the probability of an uncontained statutory violation reaching external settlement is analytically bounded. We demonstrate that this framework decouples compliance enforcement from human monitoring payroll while preserving jurisdictional portability across emerging global frameworks.

title: Quantifying the Revenue Degradation of Decoupled Recommendation and Promotion Systems: A Joint Causal Framework
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Quantifying the Revenue Degradation of Decoupled Recommendation and Promotion Systems: A Joint Causal Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed at Kohl's Corporation. This research was conducted independently and does not represent the views of the employer. No financial conflict of interest exists.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. Conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Retail personalization systems often optimize product recommendations and promotional offers separately, reflecting organizational separation between these functions. We study the revenue implications of this decoupling using a potential-outcomes framework, identifying three causal challenges: compound-treatment confounding in observational settings, suboptimal marginal optimization when product-offer interactions are non-additive, and insufficient jointaction support in logged data under deterministic allocation. We also characterize adaptive recommendation-mediated bias in direct-effect uplift measurement. When an offer changes customer behavior and an adaptive recommendation system subsequently changes the customer's product feed, the holdout difference-in-means estimator need not identify the controlled direct effect. Under a linear update model, this bias reaches 80% at high update speeds. Across fully synthetic simulations, the joint policy achieves a 9.6% to 12.7% oracle revenue advantage over the decoupled policy; the learned-policy advantage reaches 6.5% under strong interactions. A semi-synthetic experiment on the Dunnhumby dataset shows annualized gaps reaching $51.47 per household. In a logged-data simulation, doubly robust evaluation achieves lower policy-value error than direct-method evaluation at each exploration level. These findings provide simulation-based evidence that joint optimization can outperform decoupled optimization when the structural conditions studied here hold; they are not estimates of a causal revenue effect in the observed Dunnhumby transactions.

title: BioScaleML: A Lakehouse-Based Framework for,Large-Scale Biomedical Text Classification
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: BioScaleML: A Lakehouse-Based Framework for,Large-Scale Biomedical Text Classification
detail.abstract: Objective: The exponential growth of unstructured biomedical text across scientific literature, clinical narratives, and registries requires scalable, privacy-conscious informatics infrastructure. Existing solutions often rely heavily on managed cloud ecosystems, creating data governance, cost, and vendor lock-in challenges. This study presents BioScaleML, an open-source, local Lakehouse architecture designed to integrate end-to-end biomedical data management, scalable distributed processing, and reproducible machine learning (ML) pipelines within a controlled on-premises environment.,Methods: BioScaleML was engineered by coupling Apache Spark for distributed computation, Delta Lake for ACID-compliant transactional storage and schema enforcement, Hadoop for local persistence, and a PostgreSQL-backed Hive metastore for unified metadata management. The framework was evaluated across two curated biomedical text corpora totaling 49,118 documents (19,681 PubMed-style abstracts and 29,437 full-text article sections) annotated across major oncological categories (breast, lung, and prostate). Standardized Extract-Transform-Load (ETL) pipelines engineered TF-IDF feature representations, feeding reusable ML pipelines trained on local hardware.,Results: The integrated architecture enabled deterministic dataset versioning, robust schema governance, and end-to-end workflow execution on commodity infrastructure without cloud reliance. Baseline classification models—including Multinomial Logistic Regression, Linear Support Vector Machines, and Multinomial Naive Bayes—achieved consistent high-throughput classification across both corpora (reaching up to 90.6% accuracy), demonstrating that enterprise-grade data management and NLP processing can be achieved locally.,Conclusion: BioScaleML provides a practical, cost-effective blueprint for healthcare and research institutions seeking reproducible biomedical text analytics under strict data sovereignty constraints. By establishing a transaction-aware foundation, BioScaleML provides an extensible framework for scaling local informatics pipelines to advanced domain-specific language models and multi-modal clinical datasets.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become widely accessible, yet firms differ markedly in their ability to convert technical possibilities into recurrent practice. This study examines that transition through a comparative analysis of four Brazilian multinationals: Nubank, iFood, Banco do Brasil, and Petrobras. Drawing on corporate disclosures, financial and sustainability reports, technology communications, and implementation records, we reconstruct distinct deployment trajectories. Two frictions organize the analysis: discovery friction, which captures valuable applications that remain outside managerial attention, and translation friction, which concerns obstacles as selected uses are evaluated, integrated, and embedded in everyday work. The evidence shows that search architecture shapes which opportunities become visible, while contextual information, complementary resources, expertise, and governance condition their advancement. The cases reveal two pathways toward sustained incorporation: digital density, based on integrated data and technical infrastructure, and institutional scaffolding, grounded in governance, internal knowledge, and controlled development. Repeated use generates learning that reshapes subsequent choices.

title: A Versioned Terminology and Interoperability Architecture for Longitudinal Personal Laboratory Data Aligned with the European Health Data Space
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Versioned Terminology and Interoperability Architecture for Longitudinal Personal Laboratory Data Aligned with the European Health Data Space
detail.abstract: ​Objective.To design and evaluate a source-preserving, versioned terminology and interoperability architecture for longitudinal personal laboratory data, capable of alignment with EHDS and EEHRxF requirements without overwriting historical source observations — and to report the first real-world longitudinal validation of such alignment at the individual patient level.Methods.A proof-of-concept architecture was developed using a longitudinal laboratory dataset comprising 597 clinical results spanning 38 years (1988–2026) collected from multiple clinical laboratories. The design separates five distinct layers: immutable source data, semantic normalisation, terminology mapping (NPU, LOINC, UCUM and selective SNOMED CT), HL7 FHIR R4 representation and EU interoperability profiling. Mapping was performed at the level of semantically unique test combinations defined by normalised test name, specimen/system, fasting context, result type, unit and, where relevant, analytical method or calculation algorithm. Each mapping was assigned provenance, review date, confidence and status (verified/candidate/flagged). A mapping was classified as verified only when the source supported the semantic specificity required by the target terminology; when method, calibrator or calculation algorithm was insufficiently documented, the mapping was retained as candidate rather than inferred.Results.Across two mapping rounds, 122 of 290 unique test combinations (42%) were assigned verified NPU, LOINC and UCUM codes; 24 received candidate status (LOINC and UCUM verified; NPU withheld pending method, calibrator or algorithm confirmation); and 30 were flagged for source document validation. Eight case studies illustrate how contextual requirements — specimen type, measurement method, calculation algorithm, calibrator and unit representation — determine correct code selection and when deliberate non-assignment is methodologically appropriate. No source patient observation was modified. The dataset, spanning nine providers and 38 years including pre-digital records, constitutes a stringent proof-of-concept for the architecture’s robustness under conditions unavailable in curated institutional datasets.Conclusion.A source-preserving, versioned architecture constitutes a viable design pattern for patient-controlled longitudinal laboratory repositories seeking EHDS compliance. The architecture preserves source data integrity, enables incremental code verification, and accommodates evolving EEHRxF specifications without rewriting historical clinical facts — demonstrating that EHDS-aligned personal laboratory records are a present reality, not a future aspiration.

title:
The Virtual Precinct: Place-Anchored Retail,
Encounter-Based Demand, and Ground Rent as
Platform Value Capture — A CamboVerse Case

detail.title:
The Virtual Precinct: Place-Anchored Retail,
Encounter-Based Demand, and Ground Rent as
Platform Value Capture — A CamboVerse Case

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest. All authors hold appointments at the National University of Management. The first author directs the CamboVerse Center, an institute at that University; the third and fourth authors are engineers on the CamboVerse project. These are affiliations. No institutional relationship between the CamboVerse project and the Center, the University, or any external body is asserted in this paper. Participation is as individual researchers; the paper is the authors' own academic work rather than institutional output, was not produced through, reviewed by, or approved under any University governance process, and is not a University position, policy or endorsement. The authors have an evident interest in the case appearing significant; the mitigating circumstance is that the case record is public and every descriptive claim about the platform is independently checkable against the open repository and the public prototype.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Three-dimensional shops you can walk around have been announced as the future of retail twice — in virtual worlds around 2008, and in the metaverse around 2022 — and abandoned twice. We do not make the announcement a third time. We argue that both waves failed at the same point: they built places to look, not places to buy, and so never met the real questions a shop like this raises.

This paper asks those questions using CamboVerse, an open-source Virtual Cambodia — a metaverse project for the whole country, in which heritage sites are one part — with a working public prototype. Our case is the market at one of its heritage sites. When a shop sits inside a virtual version of a real place, and you reach it by visiting that place, you find products by walking past them rather than by searching. We argue that this is a property of the shop's design, not of the shopper's mood, and that it changes what people are exposed to. When the platform then routes your order to a shop in your own country, takes no payment, and charges no referral fee, three things follow. The seller is not known until checkout and has no contract with the platform. The platform earns nothing from the sale — unlike affiliate links or search ads, which charge for referrals. And the sale is recorded as ordinary domestic shopping in the buyer's country, invisible to the statistics that measure digital trade.

We then ask what such a platform could charge for, and argue that the only remaining answer is the ground: rent for stall space in a virtual market, priced on the visitors the platform's own content brings. This would keep the no-payment rule intact. It is also only a proposal, because the platform's design currently defines a router and a list of providers, and nothing that could be rented. It would inherit the problem that emptied the 2008 virtual worlds, where rent rose until merchants left. And in Cambodia it would rest on a claim that can be collected but not enforced in court.

We state each claim as either established by the design, borrowed from earlier research, following logically from stated premises, or a guess to be tested — and we keep these apart. The paper makes no empirical claim. Nothing has been sold.

Any opinions, findings, conclusions or recommendations therein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of the Office of Naval Research.

detail.abstract:
Until recently, cyberspace was considered largely a matter of low politics, the term political
scientists use to denote background conditions and routine decisions and processes. Over the last
decade, though, cyberspace, with the Internet at its core, has clearly begun to shape the domain of
high politics—that is, the national security considerations, core institutions, and decision systems
that are critical to national governments. Those governments have long held a monopoly on high
politics and are, in turn, trying to control the future of cyberspace, with, at best, very limited
success.
The field of international relations, rooted in 20th-century issues and theories, has not kept
pace with the emerging significance of cyberspace; and as the empowered non-state groups and
individuals of cyberspace and international politics now simultaneously shape one another, the
potential collisions of law, policy, and practice have barely been identified. Before the
international community can begin to minimize the negative consequences of those inevitable
collisions, it needs to understand how and where cyberspace and international relations intersect
and influence one another, and who controls those intersections.

title: Semantic Arbitrage and Feedback Instability in AI-to-AI Quotation Markets: Verified Generative Counterfactuals for Computational Theory

detail.title: Semantic Arbitrage and Feedback Instability in AI-to-AI Quotation Markets: Verified Generative Counterfactuals for Computational Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Enterprise procurement increasingly joins a buyer's generative-AI copilot with a seller's algorithmic quotation system. Although commercial requirements remain fixed, a copilot can express them through alternative request-for-quote documents that the seller interprets as different signals of urgency, switching costs, or willingness to pay. We define semantic arbitrage as the capture of quote dispersion across business-valid, truth-preserving representations of the same requirements. Historical transactions cannot identify this opportunity because each request usually reveals only one wording and one deployed price. We develop Verified Generative Counterfactuals (VGC), a generate-verify-probe-certify design that constructs the missing language interventions, audits semantic equivalence, randomizes or adaptively allocates quotation probes, and certifies the resulting operating regime. The buyer's optimal language policy has a Gibbs form. An exact value-risk identity shows that the same endogenous quote variance that creates procurement savings also generates feedback gain when the seller retrains on buyer-selected language. A unique equilibrium can therefore lose stability when gain and organizational latency cross an analytical boundary, producing endogenous quotation cycles and locally quadratic revenue loss. Semantic invariantization can guarantee stability, whereas batching may destabilize by increasing data age. A semi-synthetic study spanning 72 procurement records, 6,912 complete RFQs, four seller architectures, 400 paired search replications, and 1,584 delayed-system trajectories recovers the theoretical identities and stability frontier. The study validates the mechanism rather than estimating market prevalence. The findings connect digital representation, strategic interaction with algorithms, and performative organizational learning, while providing a rigorous, auditable governance framework for AI-mediated markets.

title: Don't Fund Winners
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Aethex Web Solutions, San Antonio, Texas, United States and University of the Incarnate Word

detail.title: Don't Fund Winners

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. No primary data were collected. The empirical section re-analyzes de-identified, publicly archived data from a previously published randomized trial (Banerjee et al. 2015; openICPSR study 113599), for which ethics approval was obtained by the original investigators.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding; it was carried out by the authors independently.

detail.abstract:
Systems that hand out money at scale, whether a bank, a grant committee, or a lending algorithm, mostly try to pick winners: they rank applicants by how well each is likely to do and fund down the list. We specify one that ranks by something else, namely how much an applicant's outcome changes because of the money. The score takes the size of that change if the venture works and multiplies it by the probability the venture works and by the probability the money would not have come from elsewhere. The objective is published before each funding cycle and can be replaced. A computer executes every decision from a written rule. People set the objective and supply facts a database cannot observe; no person chooses who is funded.

The paper decomposes real allocation systems into nine layers and proves eight results. Three restate known work. Ranking by predicted success funds the applicants who need the money least (P1). The funding cutoff is fixed by the budget, not chosen by anyone (P2). A rule that funds deterministically cannot identify a treatment effect (P3). The other five are new. A past decision can be reconstructed only if the system recorded what it knew at the time, and that record cannot be added afterwards (P4). Under several exposure limits at once the cutoff becomes applicant-specific, though a rejection still decomposes into a short list of reasons (P5). Additionality scoring concentrates the loan book in a few capital-poor districts when those districts are a minority, and only hard exposure caps contain the resulting correlated risk; a constraint on expected corpus losses does not (P6). The published objective is the operative one exactly when no step in the process is left to human discretion (P7). The people who verify facts for the system are unmeasured in the same way the applicants are, so their decisions are re-audited at random (P8). One rule connects these: the architecture and objective are disclosed in advance, and the operating parameters are committed in advance and disclosed after the cycle they governed.

The propositions are proved; whether the score itself works is not. There is one field test, a re-analysis of the Banerjee et al. (2015) Hyderabad microcredit experiment. At eighteen months, a model of which households would profit is almost uncorrelated with which households credit actually helped (r ≈ 0.05, confidence interval crossing zero). The additionality score does better (r ≈ 0.29), but a cluster-level permutation test puts it at p ≈ 0.11, short of conventional significance, and the effect has disappeared by the study's three-year endline. The paper offers a design and one supporting result; nobody has yet shown the score works.

title: NAUTILUS: An Agentic Architecture for Real-Time Supply Chain Intelligence

detail.title: NAUTILUS: An Agentic Architecture for Real-Time Supply Chain Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently with no financial relationships or organizational affiliations that could influence the study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All development and research costs were self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: Global supply chains are increasingly exposed to compounding disruptions spanning geopolitical events, commodity price volatility, natural disasters, trade policy shifts, and regulatory compliance risk. Existing enterprise procurement tools address these domains in isolation, requiring analysts to manually synthesise fragmented signals across disconnected systems. This paper presents NAUTILUS Terminal, an agentic supply chain intelligence architecture that unifies real-time multi-source data ingestion, large language model (LLM)-assisted classification and recommendation, and structured risk fusion into a single decision-support interface. The system decomposes procurement intelligence into seven autonomous API agents covering commodity pricing, geopolitical incidents, seismic events, wildfire propagation, maritime port status, foreign exchange dynamics, and trade news, whose outputs are synthesised by a central reasoning agent into actionable sourcing directives, risk scores, and compliance assessments. We describe the system architecture, data integration methodology, LLM orchestration strategy, and evaluate the system across 40 commodity categories. NAUTILUS demonstrates that agentic composition of heterogeneous live data streams, mediated by structured prompting and deterministic reasoning, produces procurement intelligence that is broader in coverage and lower in latency than conventional enterprise solutions.

title: Supply Chains as National Security Infrastructure: A Governance Framework for Strategic Supply Chain Management in Caribbean Small Island Developing States

detail.title: Supply Chains as National Security Infrastructure: A Governance Framework for Strategic Supply Chain Management in Caribbean Small Island Developing States

detail.abstract: A ministry can run out of insulin for entirely defensible reasons: the lowest bid, the leanest contract, and every rule followed. That is precisely the governance failure this paper addresses. Supply chain management in Caribbean Small Island Developing States (SIDS) has historically been conceptualised as an operational and administrative function peripheral to strategic governance. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the profound inadequacy of that conceptualisation, revealing structural vulnerabilities: overreliance on single suppliers, insufficient strategic stockpiling, weak inter-agency coordination, and the absence of risk-informed procurement frameworks, all of which had persisted largely unaddressed for decades. Drawing on frameworks from defence logistics, public administration, and supply chain resilience theory, this paper argues that supply chain governance is a national security imperative for Caribbean SIDS, and that the post-pandemic reversion to pre-crisis operational postures represents a significant and preventable governance failure. It identifies three persistent structural gaps: the primacy of efficiency over resilience in procurement frameworks; the reactive rather than structural nature of inter-agency coordination; and the absence of strategic supply chain leadership competency in public-sector career pathways. To address these gaps, the paper proposes a framework for strategic supply chain governance that encompasses formal resilience standards, permanent inter-agency coordination infrastructure, elevating supply chain leadership into the strategic conversation, and enhanced regional coordination through CARICOM mechanisms. The analysis contributes to emerging Page 2 of 25 scholarship on small-state governance, public-sector resilience, and the securitisation of critical infrastructure management.

title: QUANTUM MODULATION OF ECONOMIC STRATA

detail.title: QUANTUM MODULATION OF ECONOMIC STRATA

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Quantum Modulation of Economic Strata as the missing structural link between the author's three-tier model of infranomics (Infranomics -> Classical Economy -> Ultranomics) and the concept of Layer Zero / Axial Economy (Rakhimov, 2026f). The thesis is simple in form but consequential in scope: the quantum axis does not abolish the horizontal three-tier structure, nor does it add itself as a fourth horizontal layer. It passes through all three layers perpendicularly, preserving their ontological content while radically transforming their epistemological regime — a distinction between ontology and epistemology consistent with the broader infrastructure-as-power literature (Easterling, 2014) and with geoeconomic accounts of statecraft conducted through technical and economic instruments rather than open conflict (Blackwill and Harris, 2016). The paper explicitly demarcates the stratificational concept developed here from two surrounding bodies of work. First, the rapidly developing quantum-sovereignty literature (Oberai, Rathi, and Rao writing as Synergy Quantum, 2026; QNu Labs, 2026; Ivezic, 2025) treats quantum impact as either a sectoral policy issue (post-quantum cryptography migration, following the standards-and-timeline literature of NIST, 2024, and the threat-timeline modelling of Mosca, 2024) or as a cross-cutting cybersecurity-and-geopolitics concern, consistent with the peace-and-security framing developed by UNIDIR (2024). The present paper accepts the empirical analyses of this literature but adds the stratificational dimension that the literature lacks. Second, the term Layer Zero is well established in blockchain interoperability protocols, in cybersecurity architecture (Stamus Networks and VentureInSecurity, 2025), and in DePIN tokenomics. Priority of the term in each of those technical domains is acknowledged. The paper formalizes Quantum Modulation through the firmware metaphor: physical hardware is preserved while the cryptographic-computational code that governs its operation is rewritten. Each economic stratum receives a quantum dimension, extending the labour-displacement logic already documented for artificial intelligence (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2020) and the compute-bottleneck constraints on frontier AI capability (Whitfill and Wu, 2025) into a stratificational register. The paper additionally introduces the Anthropic Substratum as the biological invariant that lies beneath all three economic strata and falls outside quantum modulation in principle. The paper introduces the Quantum Modulation Index (QMI), extending the QSI of Layer Zero across all three economic strata with three modulation dimensions per stratum, operationalized as a nine-cell matrix per polity and illustrated through comparative case application in the manner of standard case-study design (Yin, 2018). Five anticipated objections are addressed.

detail.abstract: We study a continuous-review lost-sales inventory system with unit Poisson demand, deterministic replenishment lead time, linear holding and lost-sales costs, and a fixed setup cost per order. Two simple classical rules suffice for a uniform guarantee: order a fixed quantity when inventory position reaches a reorder point, or order a fixed quantity at regular time intervals. We prove that the infimum cost among these policies is at most 1.9602 times the optimal cost over all admissible nonanticipative replenishment policies in the standard no-disposal model, uniformly over the full nonnegative primitive space. The infinite-cycle case covers parameters for which carrying the item is uneconomic. Our policy comparisons show why the two rules complement each other: fixed cycles can be attractive when lead-time demand is substantial and lost-sales penalties are intermediate, while inventory protection is attractive for small lead-time demand or high penalties. Once configured, either rule uses a fixed lot and one ordering trigger. To our knowledge, this is the first finite worst-case approximation guarantee for the focal inventory system with an arbitrary positive fixed ordering cost, achieved by this choice of classical rules. At zero setup cost, choosing between base-stock and unit fixed-cycle policies gives a finite 1.45 guarantee. Xin (2022)'s continuous-review capped base-stock family contains these policies and therefore inherits our unit-lot guarantee. To establish the unit-lot guarantee, we develop a novel lower bound on the optimal combined holding and lost-sales cost over all admissible policies. We then batch orders to accommodate setup costs without reducing the service level, measured by the fraction of demand served.

title: A Machine Learning Framework for Predicting Student Engagement and Participation in Online IT Postgraduate Programs: Integrating Traditional Analysis with Predictive Modeling

detail.title: A Machine Learning Framework for Predicting Student Engagement and Participation in Online IT Postgraduate Programs: Integrating Traditional Analysis with Predictive Modeling
detail.abstract: Background: Online learning has become the backbone of postgraduate IT education, yet sustaining student engagement and participation remains a persistent challenge. While traditional statistical methods have identified key influencing factors, they often assume linear relationships and overlook complex interactions. Purpose: This study integrates traditional hypothesis testing with machine learning (ML) to comprehensively model the drivers of engagement and participation among IT postgraduates. The aim is to build a predictive framework that can identify at-risk learners and inform institutional interventions. Methods: A structured survey (N = 100) captured demographics, active participation, technical and personal challenges, flexibility, and engagement. We first replicated previous linear regression and difference tests, then trained Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers and regressors. Model performance was evaluated via accuracy, F1, AUC, RMSE, and feature importance was extracted. Findings: Active participation significantly predicted engagement (β = 0.475, p < .001). Challenges affected engagement but not participation directly, suggesting student resilience. Flexibility strongly enhanced participation (t = 69.65, p < .001). The Random Forest engagement classifier achieved 87% accuracy and an AUC of 0.93. Feature importance revealed that flexibility buffered the negative effects of low motivation and time management difficulties-a non-linear pattern invisible to linear models. Conclusions: ML models not only increase predictive accuracy but also uncover actionable, non-linear interactions. Institutions can use such models to build early-warning systems, while course designers should prioritise interactive activities, mobile access, and downloadable resources to mitigate technical and personal barriers.

title: Why Exceptional Founder Judgment Fails to Become

detail.abstract: The most dangerous form of founder dependence may not be created by a weak founder. It may be created by a founder who keeps being right. Founder dependence is usually treated as a problem of control, delegation, professionalization, succession, or key-person risk. Those explanations are necessary but incomplete. A scaling firm can delegate tasks, hire experienced executives, formalize processes, and distribute formal decision rights while remaining dependent on the founder for a less visible function: judgment under ambiguity. This article develops the Intelligence Transfer Problem: the persistent failure to convert founder-held interpretive and integrative judgment into an organizational capability that remains effective when the founder is absent from consequential decisions. The argument distinguishes authority transfer from judgment transfer and knowledge transfer from judgment institutionalization. It develops a causal model in which organizational complexity can outgrow institutionalized judgment capacity, producing Judgment Concentration; successful founder interventions then create Rescue Substitution, which improves short-run outcomes while suppressing independent judgment formation. The paper introduces the Founder Independence Test (FIT) and a Founder Judgment Dependence Index (FJDI) as empirical architectures for evaluating whether decision quality, speed, coherence, memory, and correctability survive founder withdrawal. The model is positioned against founder centrality, founder-control trade-offs, delegation theory, formal versus real authority, founder imprinting, organizational routines, absorptive capacity, transactive memory, people-centric scaling, and organizational replaceability. Ten propositions, rival explanations, boundary conditions, falsification tests, and a multi-method research agenda are developed. The article's core claim is not that founders should disappear. It is that organizational scale remains incomplete when consequential ambiguity must repeatedly borrow the founder's cognition.

title: A Regime-Aware, Free-Boundary Framework for Statistical Arbitrage: Kalman-Filtered Synthetic Baskets, EGARCH Volatility, Markov Regime Detection, and Optimal Stopping via Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman

detail.title: A Regime-Aware, Free-Boundary Framework for Statistical Arbitrage: Kalman-Filtered Synthetic Baskets, EGARCH Volatility, Markov Regime Detection, and Optimal Stopping via Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman

detail.abstract: We propose a statistical arbitrage framework for equity pairs and small synthetic baskets that replaces the conventional fixed-window z-score trading rule with a sequence of estimated stochastic models, each addressing a specific weakness of the standard approach. A synthetic long/short basket is constructed from Johansen cointegration loadings, restricted to the two largest-magnitude long and short weights per cluster on stability and significance grounds. The basket's hedge ratio is tracked with a Kalman filter rather than re-estimated by rolling OLS. The resulting spread's conditional volatility is modeled with an asymmetric EGARCH(1,1) process. A two-state Markov-switching model, informed by a small set of documented macro structural breaks (the 2020 COVID-19 liquidity shock and the 2024 AI-capex repricing / yen-carry unwind), gates trading activity to periods in which the spread is statistically behaving as mean-reverting. Entry and exit levels are not fixed multiples of a rolling standard deviation; they are the free boundaries of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck optimal stopping problem, solved via its Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman variational-inequality formulation with smooth-pasting conditions. A monthly seasonality overlay, shrunk toward a common prior via an empirical-Bayes (James-Stein) estimator and filtered through Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control, acts as a veto rather than an independent signal. Capital is allocated across simultaneously active spreads via a mean-variance efficient frontier (GMV/MSR), scaled by an EGARCH-based dynamic Value-at-Risk. We present the full mathematical derivation, a from-scratch numerical implementation (Kalman recursion, EGARCH quasi-MLE, Hamilton-filter EM, Engle-Granger rolling cointegration, and a scipy.integrate.solve bvp-based free-boundary solver), and a synthetic validation study confirming that the regime filter correctly de-weights the two targeted structuralbreak windows.

detail.abstract: We examine latent factor models-Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Instrumented PCA (IPCA), and Autoencoders (AE)-to explain the crosssection of international equity index returns, using a novel group of characteristics (13 firm-level factor themes built from 153 underlying characteristics, and 52 macroeconomic indicators) spanning 1995-2024. Conditional models are powerful explainers, driving pricing errors (alphas) to near zero. However, this explanatory success does not translate into robust out-of-sample predictability: only the most parsimonious linear autoencoder achieves a consistently positive, albeit modest (up to 0.45%), predictive R². We further document a previously unrecognized methodological failure of IPCA in small-N settings, where weak identification of the characteristic-loading mapping causes the model to collapse out-of-sample. Despite this divergence, interpretability analysis reveals a striking consensus: all models-linear and nonlinear-identify value, momentum, and GDP growth as the dominant drivers of risk exposure, offering guidance for taming the international factor zoo.

detail.abstract: How and why have the firms in the same industry adopted different energy efficiency (EE) approaches in different Indian states? This paper addresses this question through a comparative study of India's two largest sugar-producing states ─ Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh (UP). Based on the empirical findings, the paper argues that EE pathways should be understood as value-relative outcomes, shaped by place-based factors and co-evolutionary interactions within regional innovation ecosystems (RIE). What counts as efficient depends on the values a firm can legitimately prioritise within an RIE, where heterogenous actors negotiate values to be created and value propositions to be prioritised.

detail.abstract: Canada's $27 billion $10-a-day childcare initiative represents a generational social infrastructure investment intended to expand access and support maternal labour supply. Utilizing monthly Labour Force Survey microdata (2019-2025) and a doubly robust staggered difference-in-differences design, this paper finds no statistically significant short-run effect on maternal labour force participation within seven months of bilateral agreement signing. I discuss two key dimensions of this finding. First, the cross-provincial adoption schedule was highly compressed across eight months, which limits the available not-yet-treated control window to months 0-7 and leaves open whether longer-run effects emerge as fee cuts and capacity mature. Second, because standard survey microdata do not capture administrative waitlists or facility-level enrolment, the analysis cannot definitely decompose whether the short-run null reflects modest demand elasticity, implementation lags, or supply-side access constraints. I conclude by discussing alternative research designs--such as child age-eligibility cutoffs, actual fee reduction schedules, within-province provider variation, and linked administrative registries--and examining the institutional importance of supply-side investments alongside demand subsidies.

title: Which Factor Carries the Tail? Matched Placement of Tail Dependence in a Stylised Wrong-Way-Risk Construction

detail.title: Which Factor Carries the Tail? Matched Placement of Tail Dependence in a Stylised Wrong-Way-Risk Construction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflict of Interest

detail.abstract: Wrong-way-risk models usually summarise dependence by a single correlation or Kendall's tau. In a multi-factor setting that summary does not determine the factor through which an adverse state reaches default. We call this missing dimension the transmission channel. In a stylised two-factor construction we compare two dependence models that attach the same lower-tail copula family to default through different factors-the portfolio factor in one arm, a volatility factor in the other-calibrated to the same aggregate Kendall's tau between default and a fixed combined factor. When exposure is monotone in a single factor, and continuous at the cutoff where it reaches zero, the conditional quantile satisfies an exact one-dimensional inversion identity, PFE α = E(u *) with C(u * , p T) = (1-α)p T , with a matching quadrature identity for conditional expected exposure. Root-solving, normalisation and quadrature-refinement diagnostics are recorded separately for every value, and none of them is an error bound. At aggregate τ = 0.20 under the exact-equity payoff, moving the channel changes 99% PFE by $0.36-1.75 billion, or 7%-46%, across four factor scenarios; the difference is positive in all 24 prespecified scenario, target and payoff cells. At pairwise τ = 0.16, tail-dependent copulas produce PFE 53%-55% above Gaussian. Matching one aggregate rank statistic is a control, not an identification strategy, and it does not equalise tail intensity: the calibrated arms differ in anchor lower-tail dependence by up to 2.08×. A transition-channel mixture supplies a valid continuum between the two placements; on the reported grid the anchor is recalibrated to a common aggregate-dependence target. A placebo that drives exposure by the aggregate factor collapses the perfect-storm difference to $0.000000 billion, as the algebra requires when the two factors are equidistant from the exposure driver. No empirical claim is made. The study uses no counterparty data and no market-proxy exercise, and it makes no statement about which channel is empirically operative for any real counterparty.

detail.abstract: Programme logic, realist evaluation and Theory of Change models are well established for planning and evaluating change in complex systems, yet in practice most planning still begins with a preferred activity rather than a defined problem, and the specialist vocabulary these methods require means they are applied most consistently within resourced evaluation units, and less consistently across the many everyday planning and governance decisions made outside them. This paper sets out PEASI (Problem, Enablers, Activities, Successes, Impact), a problem-first method that distils the shared discipline of these traditions-an explicit causal chain, sensitivity to context, and an if-then Theory of Change-into a form usable by practitioners without evaluation training, developed from methodological insights accumulated across more than three decades of applied workforce, health-system and evaluation research. PEASI interrupts the conventional solution-first planning sequence by requiring Impact to be defined and Enablers mapped before Activities are chosen, and pairs this sequence with an Individual-Organisational-Global (IOG) lens that tests the resulting logic across every level of a system rather than one. The same structure that supports forward planning has carried governance and authorisation questions since early in its development, and can be read backward from Impact as a test of whether a plan is not just coherent but actionable. The paper positions PEASI against its methodological antecedents, sets out its architecture and construction sequence, its IOG and governance lenses, and its application across individual, group and digital settings, illustrated with a complete worked example from a digitally facilitated international workforce-data application, compared against a range of empirical, reconstructed and direct applications spanning workforce redesign, service delivery, education and international policy development. It closes by specifying appropriate uses and limitations, and how the method should be cited.

detail.abstract: This paper characterizes attainable consumer and producer surplus when information used for pricing must satisfy differential privacy, limiting how much it reveals about consumers' valuations. Every consumer-surplus maximizer leaves the monopolist at its uniform monopoly profit. A profit-preserving segmentation also minimizes consumer surplus under an upper-tail revenue bound. With two valuations, the set of welfare outcomes expands from a point to a line segment and then a triangle as privacy is relaxed. With any finite number of valuations, the set is a polygon, and any attainable welfare outcome can be implemented by charging a different price in each segment. Price-activation thresholds determine when disclosure changes welfare and whether consumers can gain or lose relative to uniform pricing. Sufficiently strict privacy permits only the uniform monopoly price outcome. Stronger privacy protection restricts attainable welfare outcomes and can limit the gains from price discrimination for both consumers and the producer.

detail.abstract: Income inequality within ostensibly homogeneous communities in India presents a critical development challenge that conventional aggregate measures fail to adequately capture. This study employs Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to examine the multidimensional determinants of household income distribution within a single urban community in India. Using primary survey data from 500 households, we develop and validate a comprehensive theoretical model incorporating human capital, social capital, physical capital, and institutional access as exogenous constructs, with occupational mobility and entrepreneurial activity as mediating mechanisms. Results reveal that human capital (β = 0.342, p < 0.001) and institutional access (β = 0.287, p < 0.001) exert the strongest direct effects on income outcomes, while social capital demonstrates significant indirect effects through entrepreneurial pathways (β = 0.156, p < 0.01). The model explains 58.3% of variance in household income (R² = 0.583), with acceptable predictive relevance (Q² = 0.412). Gini coefficient analysis at the micro-community level yields 0.359, indicating substantial intra-community inequality despite geographic homogeneity. These findings challenge assumptions about community-level economic homogeneity and provide actionable insights for targeted policy interventions. The study contributes methodologically by demonstrating PLS-SEM's applicability to development economics research and substantively by identifying specific capital conversion mechanisms that perpetuate or mitigate income disparities within Indian urban communities.

title: The Anatomy of Repatriation: Investor Heterogeneity in Japan’s Overseas Portfolio Adjustment

detail.title: The Anatomy of Repatriation: Investor Heterogeneity in Japan’s Overseas Portfolio Adjustment

detail.abstract: Claims that Japanese capital is 'coming home' are usually made from aggregate cross-border flows. I ask whether that aggregate sign is a sufficient statistic for repatriation. Using monthly Ministry of Finance transactions in foreign securities from January 2014 through July 2026, I separate banks, trust accounts, life insurers, and investment trusts and condition their purchases on public-data measures of short-end and long-duration Japanese government bond repricing. The internally locked primary tests compare investor-specific responses of foreign long-term-debt purchases at zero-, one-, and three-month horizons, with date-score Newey-West inference and Holm adjustment. None of the primary long-duration tests rejects equality across investors; parallel short-end tests also do not reject. The more robust fact is aggregation failure: 79.5 percent of months contain both buyers and sellers, and roughly onethird of gross core-group activity cancels within the aggregate. Protocol-designated asset-class gates locate heterogeneity elsewhere. Trust accounts differ from investment trusts in short debt after positive long-duration shocks, while banks differ from investment trusts in equities after positive short-end shocks. These gates survive yen-return and rate-differential controls, but the global-rate placebo results imply that the design cannot sharply distinguish a Japan-specific mechanism from common global-rate variation. Life insurers show an exploratory post-2022 decline in foreign-long-debt purchases that is not shared by trust accounts. I interpret the combined evidence as institution-specific asset substitution rather than synchronized repatriation. Because it comes from one official monthly transaction system and the longer-horizon tests have limited power, the design does not identify institutional motives or structural effects. Repatriation is better treated as an investor-asset-horizon classification than inferred from the sign of an aggregate flow.

detail.abstract: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) frameworks are increasingly mandated by regulation, yet Irish small and medium enterprises (SMEs) face persistent, under-theorised barriers in adopting and embedding ESG practices. This study investigates ESG drivers and novel challenges affecting Irish businesses; the characteristics of a systematic service addressing those challenges; and a structured implementation roadmap. A qualitative interpretivist design using eight semi-structured interviews with senior managers (August to October 2025) was analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Key findings reveal that ESG adoption is driven by extrinsic reputational and financial pressures; a "cascade failure problem" systematically breaks down ESG strategy between board and operational levels; Scope 3 measurement challenges are interpretive and organisational; and effective ESG services must integrate financial translation, cascading accountability, and sector benchmarking. An empirically revised P.A.C.E. (Personal Accounting Climate Economic) service framework and five-stage roadmap are presented, advancing stakeholder theory, systems thinking, and habit formation literature in SME sustainability contexts.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Ancestral Composition Distance (ACD); a bilateral measure of how similarly two countries assemble their populations from a common set of ancestral clusters. Each cluster contains countries whose native populations were culturally close around 1500. Across a global sample of country dyads (involving 163 countries), greater ancestral composition distance is systematically associated with greater contemporary cultural distance and human capital gap. More ancestrally distant countries also exhibit larger differences in income, human development, institutional characteristics, and foreign-policy positions, while trading less and exchanging fewer migrants. These relationships survive an extensive set of geographic, historical, institutional, genetic, linguistic, and religious controls, indicating that ACD captures a dimension of bilateral relatedness not summarized by standard measures. Decomposing ACD into differences already present in 1500 and differences that emerged due to post-Columbian population movements, we show that pairs whose ancestral compositions converged after 1500 are culturally closer today, conditional on their initial ancestral separation. All these results are robust to alternative ways to group countries into pre-1500 cultural clusters. We view ACD both as a useful measure for understanding contemporary cultural differences as well as a historically determined bilateral resistance term that complements conventional measures of geography, shared history, and population relatedness.

detail.abstract: We study how the contracts a prediction market chooses to offer shape trading activity and trader performance. Using the complete trading record of Polymarket's financial contracts from February 2024 to March 2026, we document a shift from one-off and monthly contracts to five-minute bets on whether asset prices would rise or fall. Trading rapidly followed each new design, increasing trading intensity as trader performance deteriorated. The share of profitable wallets fell from 60% in monthly contracts to 25% in five-minute contracts. At observed loss rates and trading intensity, $100 of capital would be depleted in 404 days in monthly contracts, compared with just 1.6 days in five-minute contracts. New accounts sustained volume as existing traders left. We develop a model that explains this pattern: a platform seeking to maximize trading volume offers shorter contracts because each new contract renews opportunities to bet on disagreement. Repeated betting then erodes the wealth of most traders, even without fees. Our findings reveal a tension between platform growth and trader performance: absent regulatory interventions, contract designs that encourage more trading can also accelerate trader losses.

detail.abstract: An attendance record can show that a task was missed while leaving unresolved why it was missed, what another party relied on, and who may authorize a response. This conceptual article examines that problem through commitment pooling: a bounded arrangement in which shared rules or practices mediate a material dependency among at least two accepted undertakings. A seven-regime map distinguishes physical and biological coordination, social norms, accepted undertakings, institutional mediation, and ethical evaluation. Practitioner accounts of Mweria and Dhome locate the inquiry in shared work and deliberation in Kenya. Constructed cases examine reliance, changing capacity, evidence, care, privacy, and the limits of decision authority. A digital trace separates protocol execution from fulfillment of accepted terms. The contribution is an integrated procedure for tracing performance, responsibility, and authority to respond within a common case history. A proposed proportionate application uses shared arrangements for routine action and focused inquiry where the decision requires it, without weakening acceptance or authority requirements. A stipulated comparison shows how alternative representations can preserve the same relevant relations; it establishes no measured advantage. Two conditional arguments and five proposed studies identify how the procedure's usefulness can be tested, including a diagnostic comparison of authority attribution. The article reports no new participant study or completed comparative validation. Its ethical inquiry also addresses needs, harms, and standing beyond accepted undertakings.

title: The Engineered Firm in the Age of AI

detail.title: The Engineered Firm in the Age of AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This perspective argues that generative and agentic AI should be treated as an enterprise-design problem rather than as a conventional technology-adoption program. It develops the concept of the engineered firm: an organization whose knowledge, coordination, governance, and judgment are deliberately configured through socio-technical architecture. The paper identifies three linked requirements. First, modular interfaces and fallbacks are needed to preserve strategic autonomy across the intelligence supply chain. Second, work systems must be redesigned around the jagged capability frontier of AI rather than around the model alone. Third, epistemic safeguards must protect human judgment from organizational cognitive atrophy. The central implication is that the CEO's role extends to the architecture through which AI enters decisions and operations: in the age of pervasive AI, firm design becomes an executive function.

title: The Auditor's Dilemma: Verifying Encrypted Credit Models While Preserving Secrecy

detail.title: The Auditor's Dilemma: Verifying Encrypted Credit Models While Preserving Secrecy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: The increasing adoption of machine learning in credit scoring offers significant advantages in predictive accuracy and efficiency but introduces a critical governance challenge: the "Auditor's Dilemma." Regulatory mandates for model explainability, fairness, and robustness necessitate rigorous third-party audits, yet these audits conflict with the proprietary nature of the models and the stringent privacy requirements of the underlying financial data. This research addresses the fundamental tension between verifiability and secrecy by exploring the application of advanced cryptographic techniques-specifically secure multi-party computation (MPC), fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs)-to enable confidential model auditing. We propose a novel framework that allows an external auditor to perform substantive testing on an encrypted credit model and its private data inputs without decrypting either, thereby ensuring the model's performance, bias, and compliance are validated without compromising business secrets or customer privacy. Our approach includes a protocol for verifying algorithmic fairness on encrypted demographic data, a method for assessing model robustness to adversarial inputs via encrypted perturbation, and a mechanism for generating publicly verifiable, non-interactive proofs of audit results. The findings demonstrate that while cryptographic overhead imposes computational costs, our framework achieves a viable balance between security and utility, offering a pragmatic pathway for financial institutions to satisfy regulatory requirements and build public trust while safeguarding their intellectual property and sensitive information. This work contributes a foundational architecture for the next generation of privacy-preserving financial audits, effectively resolving the auditor's dilemma by proving, rather than revealing, the integrity of the model.

detail.abstract: This study examines how top management team (TMT) political ideology influences supply base sustainability. Drawing on upper echelons theory, we argue that TMT's political beliefs shape their attention to and prioritization of environmental, social, and governance issues, which in turn affects firms' engagement with sustainable practices across their supply bases. We hypothesize that firms led by more liberal-leaning TMTs exhibit higher supply base sustainability. We further examine how this relationship is moderated by supply base complexity which may constrain managerial influence over sustainability outcomes. The results provide evidence consistent with the proposed relationships, suggesting that managerial ideology plays a vital role in shaping supply base sustainability beyond firm boundaries. This study has important implications for understanding how strategic leadership shapes sustainable supply chain management.

title: Artificial Entrepreneurial Cognition: Locating and Causally Steering an Opportunity Recognition Dial inside Large Language Models (LLMs)
affiliations: University of Luxembourg - Interdisciplinary Centre for Security, Reliability and Trust (SnT), University of Luxembourg, University of Amsterdam, Stanford Graduate School of Business and University of Luxembourg

detail.title: Artificial Entrepreneurial Cognition: Locating and Causally Steering an Opportunity Recognition Dial inside Large Language Models (LLMs)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: not applicable

detail.abstract: Entrepreneurial cognition is a foundation of entrepreneurship research. Yet the growing involvement of large language models (LLMs) in entrepreneurial work extends the cognition question beyond human actors to systems whose internal representations remain largely unexplored. We introduce artificial entrepreneurial cognition, the functional organisation of entrepreneurship-relevant representations and computations inside artificial intelligence (AI) systems. We bring mechanistic interpretability into entrepreneurship research through representation engineering. Focusing on opportunity recognition (OR), we construct 636 matched OR-present and OR-absent scenario pairs and recover an OR direction in Llama 3.1 8B-Instruct. Rather than infer the construct from outputs, we intervene directly on this direction, steering the model up and down along what we call the opportunity recognition dial, and its opportunity judgments shift with it. To our knowledge, this is the first causal intervention on an internal representation of an entrepreneurship construct inside an LLM. Held-out tests, lexical and topical controls, behavioural ablation, and geometric comparisons show that the direction is recoverable, consequential, and distinct from the opportunity evaluation and exploitation directions, although steering it also shifts judgments about these neighbouring stages. Recovery, signed steering, and geometric separation hold across four additional LLMs spanning different scales and families. These results give the contested distinction between opportunity recognition and evaluation a concrete representational form inside AI systems. More broadly, they establish internal representations as a new object of entrepreneurship inquiry and show how entrepreneurship theory can guide their identification, causal manipulation, and interpretation.

publicationDetails.detailsText: NYU Stern School of Business Research Paper

detail.abstract: This paper examines when reinforcement learning (RL) can outperform naive diversification in portfolio choice. We compare online actor-critic reinforcement learning with an offline Decision Transformer and the equally weighted 1/N benchmark, focusing on three determinants of outof-sample performance: learning architecture, regime information, and trading frictions. We find that conventional online actor-critic methods provide only modest improvements over 1/N , whereas the Decision Transformer delivers substantially stronger risk-adjusted performance. The value of regime information is non-monotonic: selected macroeconomic signals improve portfolio performance, but combining multiple regime-conditioning variables can materially reduce out-ofsample Sharpe ratios, consistent with an information-complexity tradeoff. These findings remain robust to alternative transaction-cost assumptions, and portfolio holdings reveal economically distinct allocation policies across architectures and information sets. Overall, reinforcement learning does not universally dominate naive diversification; its effectiveness depends critically on the interaction between learning architecture, state representation, and implementation frictions.

title: The Cost of Withdrawal: US Aid Cuts and the Unraveling of Public Health in Sub-Saharan Africa — The View from Mozambique

detail.title: The Cost of Withdrawal: US Aid Cuts and the Unraveling of Public Health in Sub-Saharan Africa — The View from Mozambique

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
Between January 2025 and mid-2026 the United States dismantled USAID, cancelled more than eighty percent of its foreign assistance awards, and replaced two decades of global health programs with a smaller system of bilateral agreements. This article examines what that withdrawal has meant for public health in sub-Saharan Africa, the region that received the largest share of American health assistance and depended on it most. It draws on peer-reviewed studies, ministry of health data, UN agency reporting, and journalism from affected communities, with Mozambique as the central case: a country where external donors financed nearly half the health sector and the United States paid for over ninety percent of HIV service delivery.

The evidence supports three conclusions. The cuts caused immediate, measurable disruption to HIV treatment, malaria control, child nutrition, and disease surveillance, at a cost in lives that the most credible estimates already put in the hundreds of thousands. The manner of the withdrawal, an overnight halt imposed on programs whose frontline delivery had been deliberately outsourced, did as much damage as the withdrawal itself. And the shock has accelerated a reckoning over aid dependence that African institutions had already begun, even though the poorest countries have no realistic means of replacing the lost financing in the near term.
