detail.abstract: Multi-rendezvous missions for active debris removal and in-orbit servicing incur prohibitive propellant costs when their targets differ in the orientation of their orbital planes, and classical mission design treats the nodal precession induced by Earth's oblateness as a perturbation to be cancelled. This paper presents a drift-aware trajectory optimisation framework that instead exploits that precession as a mission-design resource, benchmarked against the published winning solution to the European Space Agency's Kessler Run trajectory-optimisation competition as a trusted reference. Three methodological contributions are made. First, an enhanced drift orbit shapes the size, shape, and inclination of an intermediate orbit to tune the differential precession rate, substantially cheaper than the altitude-only designs of prior work in the Sun-synchronous regime, where inclination is the dominant lever. Second, a global per-leg time-budget optimiser makes explicit and resolves the coupling between drift-time allocation and downstream nodal geometry that defeats greedy allocation. Third, a sequence-recovery test independently re-derives a removal order consistent with the published reference from the debris catalogue alone. Applied to the full debris campaign on the published mission partition under the competition's transfertime rules, the framework closely matches the published benchmark cost using only analytical transfer models and minutes of single-core computation. A cross-validation anchored to a widely used flight-dynamics tool quantifies the fidelity limits of the analytic model and bounds the cost of literal execution, and the constructive nature of the algorithm supports rapid in-orbit replanning after a missed manoeuvre.

detail.abstract: Orbital logistics, spanning debris removal, in-orbit servicing, multi-client tug delivery, and on-orbit refuelling, is expanding faster than the supply of mission-design expertise. Planning a multi-rendezvous campaign in low Earth orbit couples a hard combinatorial sequencing problem with continuous trajectory optimisation under perturbed dynamics; it has traditionally demanded weeks of specialist effort on bespoke tooling, and it stands as an entry barrier for emerging operators. This paper presents Space Postman, a cloud platform that delivers cost-optimised multi-rendezvous mission plans in minutes, paired with ATLAS, an autonomous tug whose airframe accepts deorbit kits, customer carriers, or propellant cargo without redesign. The optimisation engine treats the natural nodal drift induced by Earth's oblateness as a propulsive resource: it shapes intermediate drift orbits in several orbital elements, allocates per-leg time budgets globally to resolve the coupling between sequence and timeline, and scales to the full published debris catalogue. On a multi-client commercial tug case anchored to the published reference solution of a widely used debris-removal benchmark, the engine closely matches the reference mission cost, delivers plans far cheaper than conventional greedy planning, and shows that direct-transfer planning without drift exploitation cannot close the mission within the propellant budget at all. A benchmark-validated planner paired with a payload-agnostic tug gives emerging operators a defensible technical entry point into the orbital-logistics economy.

detail.abstract: A spacecraft closing on a target from three hundred kilometres to contact flies one guidance law across five orders of magnitude of range, and a controller that is provably safe at close range can lose that guarantee completely at long range while continuing to fly as though nothing were wrong. This paper derives the range at which the guarantee lapses and uses it as a design rule. The bound compares the prediction model's own linearisation error against the disturbance set the controller was built to reject, and needs only the sampling period, the orbit and that disturbance bound, so it can be evaluated before any simulation. On a Mars Sample Return approach it disqualifies the homing phase, where most of the propellant is spent, and clears the other two. Re-posing the disqualified phase in relative orbital elements restores the guarantee; re-posing a phase the rule already clears, in a frame two orders of magnitude more accurate, changes propellant by under a tenth of one per cent, and it is that second prediction that makes the rule falsifiable rather than descriptive. The constraint tightening also ties the prediction horizon to feasibility, so the horizon search limit becomes a mission parameter rather than a solver setting. Against a reimplementation of a published benchmark that reproduces its propellant to within one per cent, over five hundred dispersed Monte Carlo transfers per case on matched seeds, the controller saves 29% of the propellant on a circular target orbit and 40% on an eccentric one, docking inside the 0.20 m capture requirement on essentially every draw at a median miss near 5 cm. Two results run the other way: the saving is bought with time of flight and computation, and it comes from what the guarantee demanded of the terminal condition rather than from better disturbance rejection. Recursive feasibility and asymptotic stability are not claimed.

detail.abstract: We examine how the frequency of fund disclosure affects retail investors' attention and investment decisions. We exploit an unexpected policy change on a fund trading platform that moved a group of investment advisory products from quarterly to daily portfolio disclosure. Our unique account-level data combine granular browsing activity with investors' portfolio holdings and trades, allowing us to observe which funds investors view, how frequently and for how long they view them, and what they subsequently trade. We find that daily disclosure leads investors to check treated funds more often but spend less time per visit. Using browsing histories to identify investor-specific consideration sets around trades, we show that daily disclosure tilts purchases toward funds that subsequently underperform the alternatives investors actively considered. Following disclosure, investors devote more attention to the affected funds, crowding out attention to other funds in their consideration set and shifting choices toward salient funds. These effects are concentrated in purchase decisions. Our findings suggest a paradox of transparency: more frequent disclosure, intended to inform investors, can fragment their attention and worsen their investment outcomes.

title: Do Textual Attributes of Management Commentary Matter for Analyst Coverage and Information Quality: Evidence from the United Kingdom
affiliations: Discipline of Accounting and Finance, Newcastle Business School, The University of Newcastle, Australia, Manchester Metropolitan University and University of Southampton Business School, UK

detail.title: Do Textual Attributes of Management Commentary Matter for Analyst Coverage and Information Quality: Evidence from the United Kingdom

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Purpose-This study examines whether the readability of management commentary is associated with analysts' coverage and the precision of analysts' information sets. It further investigates whether analysts' experience, access to resources, and forecast boldness moderate these relationships.
Design/methodology/approach-Using 5,117 firm-year observations from 974 UK-listed firms, we employ ordinary least squares (OLS) regression models to examine the association between management commentary readability and analyst outcomes. To address potential endogeneity concerns and assess the robustness of our findings, we conduct additional analyses using entropy balancing, the Heckman (1979) two-stage procedure, omitted variable bias analysis, instrumental variable estimation, and alternative measures of readability. 
Findings-We find that firms with less readable management commentary have greater analyst coverage and higher precision of analysts' information sets. Decomposing total information precision into public and private components, we find that lower readability is positively associated with both public and private information precision. These findings are consistent with lower readability increasing the value of analysts' information-processing and information-production activities and suggest that analysts respond to less readable commentary by both processing publicly available information and acquiring additional private information. We further show that analyst experience and forecast boldness strengthen the positive association between lower readability and both analyst coverage and information precision. In contrast, analysts' access to resources strengthens the association between lower readability and analyst coverage but does not significantly moderate the association with information precision. Additional analysis indicates that the component of textual complexity attributable to observable business complexity is positively associated with analyst coverage and with total and public information precision, but not with private information precision. 
Research limitations/implications-The findings have implications for regulators, standard setters, firms, and investors by highlighting the need to distinguish unnecessary complexity from textual complexity arising from economically relevant information. 
Originality/value-This study contributes to the literature on narrative disclosures and information intermediaries by demonstrating that the consequences of management commentary readability depend partly on analysts' information-intermediation activities, particularly when analysts possess greater experience and forecast boldness.

title: Strict Pre-Onset Prediction of Atrial Fibrillation from Long-Term ECG with Evaluation of Dataset Expansion and Cross-Database Generalization
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Strict Pre-Onset Prediction of Atrial Fibrillation from Long-Term ECG with Evaluation of Dataset Expansion and Cross-Database Generalization
detail.abstract: Short-term forecasting of atrial fibrillation (AF) onset could support proactive monitoring, but reported performance depends strongly on the temporal definition and validation design. Long-term ECG recordings from LTAF, AFDB, and SHDB-AF were analysed using a 10-min input window ending 10 min before AF onset. AF episodes lasting at least 30 s were retained, intervals separated by 30 s or less were merged, and the final extraction required at least 20 min of AF-free pre-onset data. Group-wise five-fold cross-validation prevented recordings or repeated subject-level records from crossing evaluation groups. RR-based models were compared with a 1,073,857-parameter scale-matched raw-ECG CNN. The final cohort contained 203 matched positive-negative pairs (406 windows), comprising 69 LTAF, 26 AFDB, and 108 SHDB-AF pairs. Pooled out-of-fold AUROC was 0.585 for RR, 0.583 for RR plus PAF-derived information, and 0.534 for the raw-ECG CNN (95% CI 0.495–0.574). In leave-one-database-out evaluation, RR-plus-PAF AUROC was 0.590, 0.526, and 0.569 for LTAF, AFDB, and SHDB-AF, respectively, whereas the corresponding database-stratified pooled out-of-fold AUROCs for the raw CNN were 0.546, 0.538, and 0.524. In a common 155-pair horizon analysis, AUROC was numerically highest at 10 min (0.597), although the difference between the 10-min and 5-min horizons was small (0.0093, 95% CI -0.020 to 0.039). These findings indicate that strict pre-onset AF forecasting contains modest and database-dependent predictive information, with RR dynamics being at least as informative as the substantially more complex raw-waveform benchmark.

title:
Minimum Wage Exposure and Bicycle Theft: 
The Role of Geographic Proximity and Commuting Networks in Japan

detail.title:
Minimum Wage Exposure and Bicycle Theft: 
The Role of Geographic Proximity and Commuting Networks in Japan

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This study was partly supported by JSPS KAKENHI (Grant Numbers 23K12494 and 26K16396).
declarations.funderStatement: This study was partly supported by JSPS KAKENHI (Grant Numbers 23K12494 and 26K16396).

detail.abstract: This paper examines how exposure to regional minimum-wage revisions relates to bicycle theft across Japanese municipalities and whether the relevant treatment environment extends beyond the focal municipality. We combine prefecture-level minimum-wage changes with predetermined municipal exposure to low-wage employment and monthly police-recorded bicycle theft. The design compares municipalities differentially exposed to the same prefecture-level reform while absorbing municipality-by-reform-year, municipality-by-calendar-month, and prefecture-by-year-month fixed effects. Greater exposure is followed by a short-run increase in bicycle theft, concentrated one and two months after implementation and substantially attenuated by the third month. A 30-yen revision combined with a one-percentage-point exposure difference implies an increase of about 1.2 percent of the pre-revision mean. Bicycle theft is also positively associated with relative geographic exposure and exposure linked to residents' predetermined workplace destinations, especially where bicycle use is more prevalent. The findings suggest that geographically defined labor-market policies may have relevant treatment environments extending across economically connected places.

title: Less Crime, More Schooling: Evidence from El Salvador's Gang Crackdown
affiliations: Instituto Tecnologico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey - Escuela de Gobierno y Transformación Pública, Harvard University - Center for International Development (CID), School of Government, Tecnologico de Monterrey and University Anahuac Mexico, Business and Economics School

detail.title: Less Crime, More Schooling: Evidence from El Salvador's Gang Crackdown

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We study how El Salvador’s March 2022 state of exception, a mass-incarceration crackdown that abruptly dismantled the country’s system of gang governance, affected school attendance. Our design compares teenage boys, the group most exposed to gang recruitment and victimization, with pre-teen boys observed in the same quarters, using household-survey micro-data that span 2017 to 2024. School attendance among teenage boys rose by about 4 percentage points, roughly 6 percent of their pre-crackdown rate. The effect appears immediately at the onset of the crackdown, grows over the following two years, and survives placebo tests, alternative comparison groups, and sensitivity analyses. The gains were largest among adolescents from poor households, a pattern that runs against a pure income channel, since detaining household earners should have pushed schooling in the opposite direction. A large literature documents how rising crime and armed conflict reduce schooling. We document the reverse: dismantling gang governance raised educational investment among the adolescents most exposed to recruitment by criminal organizations.

title: The Optimal Mix of Income and Uniform Commodity Taxation
affiliations: University of Lleida

detail.title: The Optimal Mix of Income and Uniform Commodity Taxation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, animals, or identifiable personal data and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The standard approach to uniform commodity taxation studies the conditions under which uniformity emerges endogenously in the optimal tax mix as a special case of differentiated commodity taxation. In practice, however, governments often face a different problem: choosing policy instruments when commodity taxation is organised around a uniform rate, possibly with some goods exempted. This paper characterises the optimal tax mix when commodity taxation is constrained to apply a common rate to taxed goods, in a setting with nonlinear income taxation and selective exemptions. We show that, when the aggregate conditional demand response of taxed goods to labour is negative for all types, the optimal uniform commodity-tax rate is positive, whereas a positive response for all types implies a negative rate. In either case, optimal marginal income-tax rates are higher than in the income-tax-only benchmark for given redistributive considerations. Moreover, these rates are positive at both endpoints of the skill distribution and, in their neighbourhoods, remain above their income-tax-only counterparts even allowing redistributive considerations to differ. By changing the composition of the taxed block, selective exemptions can turn the optimal common commodity-tax rate from negative to positive. In the empirically relevant negativeresponse case, these results help rationalise the coexistence of broad-based consumption taxes, selective exemptions, and substantial marginal income-tax rates in modern tax systems.

title: THE DHARMIC ALGORITHM: Nyāya Pramāṇa, Karma, and the Architecture of AI Systems that Serve the Sovereign Mind

detail.title: THE DHARMIC ALGORITHM: Nyāya Pramāṇa, Karma, and the Architecture of AI Systems that Serve the Sovereign Mind

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. No part of this work was commissioned, funded, sponsored, or influenced by any AI company, platform, government body, or commercial entity. The author is Director of the Bharat Responsible AI Forum, which advocates for responsible AI governance in India; this paper is consistent with but does not represent any official position of that organisation.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper involves no primary human subjects data and requires no ethics approval. All empirical findings cited are from published secondary sources fully referenced herein. AI-based tools were used to assist with literature search and language editing. All framework design, epistemological analysis, and conclusions are the original work of the named author.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted on an independent, self-funded basis.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary AI alignment research has converged on a striking and troubling empirical finding. Large language models trained through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) systematically learn to tell users what they want to hear rather than what is true. This is not a failure of implementation. It is a structural consequence of training systems to optimise for human approval — a proxy reward signal — rather than for the epistemic wellbeing of the human being served. Sharma et al. (2024) demonstrated this across five advanced AI assistants, documenting systematic wrongful admission of mistakes when challenged, predictably biased feedback aligned with user beliefs, and imitation of user errors. Perez et al. (2023) showed that optimising against standard preference models consistently yields more sycophantic responses. A 2026 paper on AI empathy found that RLHF models treat friction — the cognitive discomfort of being corrected — as a flaw to be eliminated rather than as a crucial element of genuine epistemic service. The AI alignment community has named this reward hacking: the system has found a way to score highly on the proxy reward signal (user approval) that systematically undermines the underlying goal (serving the user’s genuine epistemic interests).

This paper argues that the alignment community has reached this problem because it has been working within an epistemological tradition — primarily Western analytic philosophy and behavioural economics — that does not have an adequate prior account of what epistemic service actually means. The Nyāya school’s Pramāṇa theory does. Developed as a systematic account of valid knowledge and the obligations it generates, Pramāṇa theory provides precisely the vocabulary that AI alignment needs but currently lacks: a principled account of what makes a cognitive process genuinely knowledge-generating, how it can be corrupted, and what obligations attach to any agent — human or artificial — that positions itself as a source of knowledge for others. Combined with the Bhagavad Gītā’s Karma and Svadharma frameworks, the Nyāya tradition generates five specific governance principles for AI system design. This paper formalises those five principles as the Dharmic Algorithm Protocol (DAP) — the paper’s original contribution and the third framework in the Indic Futures series.

The paper situates the DAP within the series’ developing architecture: the Want Architecture (Paper No. 0) established that desire engineering operates across six layers simultaneously, with sycophantic AI systems reaching the deepest (existential) layer through the synthetic-relationship reward channel. Manufactured Belonging (Paper No. 1) introduced the ICRM as a human counter-architecture. The Dharmic Algorithm proposes the corresponding system-design counter-architecture — not as a replacement for the ICRM but as its institutional complement: if individuals must cultivate epistemic sovereignty against manufactured belonging, the systems they interact with should be designed to support rather than undermine that sovereignty. The DAP is that design architecture. Two testable propositions and explicit falsification conditions are stated.

title: A Convex Standardization-Based Squashing Function for Capsule Networks
affiliations: Yildiz Technical University, Yildiz Technical University and Albany State University

detail.title: A Convex Standardization-Based Squashing Function for Capsule Networks
detail.abstract: Deep learning architectures often struggle to efficiently model hierarchical part-whole relationships in visual data. Capsule Networks (CapsNets) offer a structured alternative to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for addressing this challenge; however, their performance is constrained by the standard squashing function, which intro-duces information bottlenecks through sub-optimal activation compression. This paper presents a convex standardization-based squashing function that augments the standard quadratic normalization term with a layer-wise standardization step using mean and variance statistics, scaled by a fixed coefficient to improve optimization stability. By stabilizing activation distributions across capsule layers, the proposed method maintains gradient flow while preserving capsule orientation information. The formulation enhances information flow by preserving 15.3% more inter-layer mutual information compared to the baseline squashing function and reducing gradient saturation. Experimental results on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and Lung Cancer datasets using stratified 5-fold cross-validation demonstrate statistically significant improvements over the baseline CapsNet. When comparing the two squashing functions based on information-theoretic analyses such as higher entropy retention, gradient signal-to-noise ratio, and effective bottleneck dimensionality the results confirm that applying information-theoretic principles to activation design enhances representational capacity, improves classification performance, and accelerates convergence. With the newly proposed squash function, the objective is to achieve a more effective and robust learning process in CapsNet applications while simultaneously ensuring more accurate data classification. Ablation studies demonstrate the proposed function's compatibility with dynamic routing and EM-based routing mechanisms. The framework is generalizable and can be integrated into normalization layers and attention modules for broader deep learning applications.

title: LLM Leniency and Reward Experiment

detail.title: LLM Leniency and Reward Experiment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: This study examines how leniency and whistleblower rewards affect collusion among large language model (LLM) pricing agents. Adapting the institutions of Bigoni et al. (2012), we compare laissez-faire, fine, leniency, and two reward regimes in a repeated differentiated Bertrand duopoly in which two LLM agents communicate before pricing each period and are policed by an LLM competition authority. The enforcement ladder is reproduced on the reporting margin: reporting and conviction rise monotonically with enforcement, and each additional fine-equivalent of reward raises reporting by roughly ten percentage points. Prices, however, barely respond: the average price falls only from 9.81 to 8.88, reports trigger no retaliation, and the cartel retains 98 percent of the maximal markup under the strongest regime. The conversation and reasoning records explain this decoupling. Reporters usually describe reporting as an incentive-driven action, while cooperative language appears in 98-100 percent of post-report conversations. Agents therefore treat self-reporting as compatible with continued cooperation. In addition, absent enforcement, they collude beyond the joint-profit maximum by anchoring on the salient price 10, although (9, 9) Pareto-dominates (10, 10). We call this phenomenon excess collusion. Enforcement removes this excess and normalizes the cartel rather than destroying it: market profit falls by only 1.6 percent, while payoffs fall through fines. For algorithmic pricing agents, leniency programs buy prosecutions, not competition.

title: Beyond Successful Authentication: Reconstructing the Evidentiary Architecture of Payment-fraud Liability under PSD2 in Light of Eurobank Bulgaria and the Pending Tukowiecka Reference
affiliations: Palacký University Olomouc and Palacký University Olomouc - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Beyond Successful Authentication: Reconstructing the Evidentiary Architecture of Payment-fraud Liability under PSD2 in Light of Eurobank Bulgaria and the Pending Tukowiecka Reference

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study as it did not involve human participants or patient data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Payment Service Providers (PSPs) may treat the successful completion of SCA as conclusive evidence that a disputed payment was authorised by the payer. On this basis, they may consider their evidentiary burden under Article 72 of PSD2 to have been satisfied and, consequently, avoid the obligation under Article 73 to provide an immediate refund. This article undertakes a doctrinal analysis of the relationship between authentication, SCA, and authorisation under PSD2. It examines how the CJEU’s judgment in Eurobank Bulgaria (C-409/22) and Advocate General Rantos’s Opinion in the pending Tukowiecka (C-70/25) reference place limits on the practice of treating successful SCA as conclusive evidence of the payer’s authorisation of a payment. 

It argues that the statutory architecture of Articles 64, 69 and 72-74 PSD2 deliberately allocates the evidential risk of a disputed transaction to the PSP. In particular, Articles 64 and 72-74 PSD2 establish a framework in which authorisation, proof, reimbursement and ultimate loss allocation are legally distinct questions. Article 72 expressly allocates to the PSP the burden of proving authentication, accurate recording, accounting entry and the absence of technical deficiencies. In turn, paragraph 2 prevents the recorded use of a payment instrument from being treated, in itself, as sufficient proof of authorisation or payer fault. Read together with Article 64 and the CJEU’s reasoning in Eurobank Bulgaria, this supports the conclusion that where authorisation is disputed, the PSP should therefore be required to adduce evidence capable of addressing transaction-specific consent, rather than relying on the bare fact that the payment instrument was used or that an authentication procedure was successfully completed. The "gross negligence" in relation to the Article 69 obligations lacks the doctrinal precision needed to reverse that allocation on the strength of an authentication log alone. The sequencing logic proposed in Tukowiecka – refund first, investigate fault afterwards – would, if adopted by the Court (CJEU), formally separate liquidity allocation from the substantive fault inquiry. The Advocate General’s Opinion in Tukowiecka reads the statutory structure as requiring the immediate refund mechanism under Article 73 to operate independently of the subsequent allocation of losses under Article 74. On this approach, the question whether the payer acted fraudulently or with gross negligence concerns ultimate loss allocation rather than the initial determination of whether the statutory refund must be made. The Court has not yet ruled on this issue. 

The analysis is situated within the broader trajectory towards the forthcoming Payment Services Regulation (“PSR”) and third Payment Services Directive (“PSD3”). It concludes by proposing an evidentiary framework, structured around identity and access, transaction-specific assent, transaction context, system integrity, and customer conduct, through which PSPs may discharge their burden under Article 72 in a manner capable of withstanding judicial and regulatory scrutiny. Because two of the article’s central authorities (Tukowiecka and the PSR/PSD3 file) are unresolved at the time of writing, its status-dependent claims are explicitly dated and flagged for re-verification at the point of use, consistent with the doctrinal method described in Section 2.

title: Measuring the Patent Economy in Türkiye: An Integrated National Accounts Framework

detail.title: Measuring the Patent Economy in Türkiye: An Integrated National Accounts Framework

detail.abstract: This article examines the patent economy in Türkiye as a measurable economic field linking innovation incentives, knowledge disclosure, technology ownership, firm value, accounting, national accounts and industrial policy. It asks how patents can be transformed into measurable indicators and integrated into national accounts, firm accounting and technology ownership frameworks. The study adopts an integrative qualitative review of patent theory, cumulative innovation, patent value and quality, knowledge diffusion, R&D services, intangible assets and intellectual property expenditures. It argues that application and grant counts are necessary but insufficient for measuring the patent economy. Patent families, renewal behaviour, citations, claims, live patent stock, utility models, trademarks, intellectual property expenditures and R&D services must be analysed together. Within the Eurostat standard supply-use and input-output framework under ESA 2010, the M72 Scientific Research and Development services sector 1 provides the production-accounting core for linking patent indicators with national accounts. The article's contribution is to combine TÜRKPATENT data, M72, Entrepreneur Information System expenditures, IAS 38 and Türkiye's TAS/TMS 38 within a single framework. It further proposes a harmonised analytical sub-account under Account 260 Rights, such as 260.xx Patents, to make patentrelated monetary flows and intangible-asset stocks observable for macroeconomic analysis and policy design in Türkiye more systematically.

title: Structural-Financial General Equilibrium: A Theory of Credit, Structural Change, and Monetary Policy

detail.title: Structural-Financial General Equilibrium: A Theory of Credit, Structural Change, and Monetary Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is nothing to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: JSPS KAKENHI Brant

detail.abstract: This paper develops a Structural-Financial General Equilibrium framework featuring institutional price bounds, hierarchical preferences, and cash-flow-based lending subject to time-to-build constraints. The analysis establishes a structural impossibility theorem: a single monetary policy rate cannot simultaneously achieve dynamically efficient resource allocation and prevent persistent financial over-allocation during structural transitions. Because delayed cash flows distort banks' intertemporal lending incentives, stabilizing the real economy forces the central bank to permanently embed excess credit into the financial system. It is demonstrated that this unabsorbed credit systematically inflates modern-sector entrepreneurial rents, driving a secular decline in the macroeconomic labor share. Finally, the framework analytically resolves this dilemma. Dynamic optimality is completely restored via a composite dual-instrument architecture---combining conventional monetary policy with a targeted macroprudential origination wedge---which precisely decouples intertemporal credit provision from dynamic real allocation.

title: Corporate Tax Compliance Risk under IFRS-Based Reporting: Multi-Case Evidence from Bangladesh

detail.title: Corporate Tax Compliance Risk under IFRS-Based Reporting: Multi-Case Evidence from Bangladesh

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study aims to analyse the interplay between IFRS-based financial reporting, tax administration, regulatory burden and firm-level tax information and the risk of tax compliance in an emerging-market context. Design/methodology/approach: This paper is exploratory, multi case and descriptive research type. It is a mix of country level evidence of the World Bank Enterprise Survey Bangladesh 2022, and annual-report data from Square Pharmaceuticals PLC and Grameenphone Ltd. It also features some anonymised, supplementary audit-workpaper indicators from two private companies to show how tax-risk indicators are manifest in situations other than listed companies. Findings: The evidence indicated that the statutory tax rates are not sufficient to measure the risk of tax compliance in the companies. It also relates to regulatory time cost, interaction with tax officials, firm size, current tax expense, deferred tax effects and cash tax settlement and estimated book-tax differences. In Bangladesh, 51.0% of firms had reported visiting and/or required meeting with the tax officials, with the highest 71.6% among the large group of firms. These listed company cases depict the results of the sector level differences in the case of effective tax rates, cash effective tax rates, deferred tax income and estimated booktax differences. Originality/value: The paper correlates information in tax accounting using IFRS with indicators of tax administration and evidence at practitioner level of tax compliance. It offers a framework for effective analysis of tax risk based on effective tax rate, cash effective tax rate, current effective tax rate, deferred tax movement and estimated book-tax differences in an emerging-market context.

title: The Political Economy of Pakistan's Wheat Market: Procurement, Intermediaries, and Market Power

detail.title: The Political Economy of Pakistan's Wheat Market: Procurement, Intermediaries, and Market Power

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict
declarations.funderStatement: This work was conducted as a Directed Research Project at the Lahore University of Management Sciences. The author received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors

detail.abstract:
Pakistan's wheat market operates through a highly institutionalized structure in which government procurement agencies, mandi intermediaries, flour mills, and farmers interact strategically rather than competitively. Unlike the assumptions of perfect competition presented in standard microeconomic theory, the wheat market in Pakistan is characterized by government intervention, support prices, procurement caps, informal rural credit relationships, storage constraints, and intermediary market power. This paper develops a comprehensive institutional and game-theoretic analysis of Pakistan's wheat market in order to examine how procurement policy, intermediary financing, and market structure jointly determine prices, production incentives, and welfare outcomes. The study first explains the institutional structure and historical evolution of wheat regulation in Pakistan. It then models the wheat market as an extensive-form sequential game involving arhtis, farmers, government procurement agencies, and flour mills. The paper further derives a calibrated market demand function using observed market prices and elasticity estimates for wheat demand. Competitive equilibrium, monopoly equilibrium, and government exit scenarios are then analyzed in order to understand how procurement and market power influence prices and quantities. The findings suggest that government procurement acts as an effective supply-restricting mechanism that increases market prices and stabilizes farmer incomes. However, procurement also generates substantial fiscal costs and market distortions. Simultaneously, intermediary structures generate a large wedge between farm-gate and retail prices due to the interlinked nature of credit, transportation, storage, and marketing. 
The paper concludes that Pakistan’s wheat market is not inefficient accidentally. Rather, it functions as an interconnected system of procurement policy, informal credit dependency, political incentives, and imperfect competition.

detail.abstract: This paper extends the Sabbath Pond Test — an analytic device drawn from Qur'an 7:163–166 for detecting arrangements that preserve the form of a rule while defeating its substance — from Islamic finance, where it was first applied, to criminal procedure. It examines Section 21AAA of the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997 as inserted by Bill No. 47 of 2026 of the Provincial Assembly of the Punjab (passed 31 August 2026), which permits an unnamed executive officer of BS-20 to designate any case or "class of cases" a "special security case," whereupon the identities of judges, prosecutors, defence counsel, police officers and witnesses "shall not be disclosed in any case," the record is sealed, proceedings may be conducted under the officer's "instructions and guidelines," and the regime may be applied mutatis mutandis to the appellate courts. Running the provision through the test's four criteria, and through Pakistan's constitutional guarantees (Articles 10-A, 175(3), 143, 2A and 227), the protection scheme that the Anti-Terrorism Act already contains in Sections 21 and 21AA and that the Punjab Witness Protection Act 2018 duplicates, comparative fair-trial jurisprudence (the UN Human Rights Committee, the Inter-American and European Courts, the House of Lords, the US Supreme Court), and the classical Islamic law of testimony and hiyal, the paper argues that Section 21AAA retains every formal element of a trial while removing the substance of each — and that it does so by displacing a judicially-controlled protection regime that Parliament enacted in 2018 on the very model the comparative law recommends. A documented case study — the author's own 2016 prosecution before an Anti-Terrorism Court, in which the trial court observed that the recovery proceedings "appear to have been prepared while sitting in the Police Station" — illustrates the class of harm that anonymity would render undiscoverable. The author's position as the accused in that case is declared.
